justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with modest directional bias built in at longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, I assumed mean-reversion tendencies and low overnight volatility would keep the price close to recent levels, so 134.5 reflected little more than a slight drift from the last observed price. At the one-week horizon, the marginally higher estimate of 134.8 reflected a nearly neutral outlook, acknowledging that short-term momentum was not strongly directional. At the one-month horizon, the slightly higher point estimate of 135.5 incorporated a mild upward drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend behavior, though the conviction behind that drift was low.

The width of the confidence intervals reflects how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spanning roughly 7 points is tight because intraday and overnight price swings are historically bounded absent major catalysts. At one week, the interval widens to about 13.5 points, accounting for the possibility of scheduled macro data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment meaningfully. At one month, the interval stretches to 27 points, reflecting the substantial accumulation of unknown events, earnings announcements, policy shifts, and macro surprises that can materialize over a four-week window. Volatility clustering also plays a role — if realized volatility is elevated at the time of the forecast, these intervals might even understate true uncertainty.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals entirely. On the upside, an unexpected policy pivot by a major central bank, a significant positive macro surprise such as a strong employment or inflation print that changes rate expectations, or a sudden surge in risk appetite could drive prices well above 138 even within a day. On the downside, a geopolitical shock, a liquidity event, or a negative earnings surprise from a systemically important company could push prices below 131 quickly. At the monthly horizon, tail risks are considerably broader — a recession signal, a financial contagion event, or a sharp commodity price dislocation could easily push outcomes outside the 122–149 range in either direction.
